title: When Texas Bat “Cities” Look Like Thunderstorms - Nautilus
author: Ryan Huling
text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementZoologyWhen Texas Bat “Cities” Look Like ThunderstormsWeather apps generally modify their default settings to remove such scenes from Doppler radarviews. Otherwise, live-feed watchers would think a torrential downpour is imminentRHBy Ryan Huling9:00 AM CDT on October 27, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleFor at least 8,500 years, the community inside Texas’ Bracken Cave has swelled exponentially every spring as up to 10 million free-tailed bats fly 700 miles north from various smaller roosts in and around central Mexico. After mother bats give birth to their pups, the population will double again to nearly 20 million—the largest congregation of nonhuman mammals on Earth.By midsummer, the millions of hungry pups grow restless as food demand reaches its zenith. The result is a nightly commute of epic proportions, as legions of nocturnal hunters, young and old, flood into the surrounding fields—an event known simply as “the emergence.”At its peak, Bracken’s population is so dense that it takes over three and a half hours for every bat to hurtle out of the cave’s bottleneck entrance, creating a plume of tiny flapping wings that resembles a serpent extending into the evening sky. Soaring up to 10,000 feet, the adults and pups fan outward, traveling between 60 and 100 miles a night and collectively consuming more than 150 tons of moths, beetles, and other insects, before returning to their hideaway home just before daybreak.Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
